title: Phase 1 · Stage 3: Methods
summary: Break the loop into named methods with parameters, out values, tuples and defaults, and add a fine calculator.

steps.title: One job per method
body: The loop now does everything at once: split, validate, count and print. As Shelfwise grows that becomes unreadable. A **method** gives a piece of work a name, inputs and an output:
var (command, rest) = SplitCommand(line);      // deconstruct the tuple

Methods written after the top-level statements are **local functions**: they can read and change the variables declared above them (`books`, `copies`), which is convenient now and something Phase 2 will tidy away.
Three parameter tools you will use in this stage:
- a **tuple** return gives back two values at once, as above;
- an **out** parameter hands back extra results: `string? ValidateBook(string[] parts, out int year, out int count)` returns an error message (or `null`) *and* the parsed numbers;
- an **optional** parameter has a default: `decimal FineFor(int daysLate, decimal perDay = 0.50m)` can be called as `FineFor(3)` or `FineFor(3, 0.25m)`.

code: decimal Fine(int days, decimal perDay = 0.50m) => Math.Min(days * perDay, 10.00m);
steps.explain: The default `0.50m` is used when the second argument is left out. `Math.Min` caps the fine at 10.00. A decimal keeps the scale of its operands, so `3 * 0.50m` prints as `1.50`.

steps.prompt: Complete the method so the caller gets both the error and the parsed number.
code: if (!int.TryParse(text, out __2__) || count < 1) return "copies must be at least 1";
steps.explain: `out` lets a method hand back a value through a parameter. `null` means *no error*, which is why the return type is `string?`.

steps.prompt: Which call is **not** allowed for `string Plural(int n, string word)`?
steps.explain: Positional arguments must be in order: `n` first. Named arguments (`word:`) may come in any order. `Plural(n: 3, "days")` is fine because the named argument is in its own position.

steps.title: Extract methods and add fines
prompt: Refactor the loop into methods, then add a new command. Everything from stage 2 must behave exactly as before.
Write these methods (after the loop, as local functions):
| `(string Command, string Args) SplitCommand(string text)` | lower-cased command word and trimmed rest |
| `string AddBook(string text)` | validates and counts a book, returns the message to print |
| `string? ValidateBook(string[] parts, out int year, out int count)` | the error text without `Error: `, or `null` |
| `string Plural(int n, string word)` | `1 day`, `3 days`: adds an `s` unless `n` is 1 |
| `decimal FineFor(int daysLate, decimal perDay = 0.50m)` | `daysLate * perDay`, capped at `10.00` |

New command `fine <days>`: prints `Fine for 3 days late: $1.50` (use `Plural`, so 1 gives `1 day`). If the days are not a whole number of at least 0: `Error: use fine <days late>`. Add `fine` to `help`: `Commands: add, stats, fine, help, quit`.
Shelfwise v1. Type help for commands.
Commands: add, stats, fine, help, quit

string? ValidateBook(string[] parts, out int year, out int count)
if (!int.TryParse(parts[3], out year) || year < 1450 || year > 2026) return "year must be a number from 1450 to 2026";
if (!int.TryParse(parts[4], out count) || count < 1) return "copies must be a whole number of at least 1";

require.message: ValidateBook hands back numbers with out parameters
FineFor has an optional perDay parameter

hints: Move each block of the loop into a method and call it: the `add` case becomes `Console.WriteLine(AddBook(rest));`.
`ValidateBook` must assign both `out` parameters on every path: start with `year = 0; count = 0;`, then `int.TryParse(parts[3], out year)`.
`decimal FineFor(int daysLate, decimal perDay = 0.50m) => Math.Min(daysLate * perDay, 10.00m);` and the message is `$"Fine for {Plural(days, "day")} late: {FineFor(days):C}"`.
